summary.text: A 52-year-old undomiciled man with obesity and a history of nicotine dependence and polysubstance abuse presented to an outside hospital with shortness of breath and lower extremity edema. He was diagnosed with acute decompensated heart failure and hypoxic respiratory failure. TTE showed right heart dilatation and severe tricuspid regurgitation, and a ventilation-perfusion scan indicated a high probability of acute pulmonary embolism. Anticoagulation was started and symptoms improved.

He later underwent coronary angiography and RHC, showing angiographically normal coronary arteries and severe pulmonary hypertension due to CTEPH, and was medically managed with riociguat and anticoagulation. Six months later a repeat ventilation-perfusion scan and TTE gave similar results; repeat RHC showed severe pre- and postcapillary pulmonary hypertension with PVR 8.6 Wood units, and pulmonary angiography showed pulmonary artery dilatation, occlusions and perfusion defects.

He underwent pulmonary thromboendarterectomy without complication. Follow-up RHC approximately 3 months after PTE showed improved pulmonary hemodynamics with PVR reduced to 4.8 Wood units, and follow-up pulmonary angiography showed reduced thrombotic burden.

For research purposes he underwent adenosine stress perfusion CMR approximately 1 month before PTE and 1 year after PTE. Stress biventricular MBF and MPR were significantly reduced before PTE; after PTE, RV and LV perfusion improved and both ventricle volumes were reduced, especially RV volumes.

summary.text: A 62-year-old woman with obesity and a past medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypothyroidism, stroke and chronic kidney disease presented to an outside health care facility with dry cough, fatigue and shortness of breath. She was initially diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia but did not improve with multiple courses of antibiotics and corticosteroids.

TTE showed a severely dilated and dysfunctional RV with septal flattening, and helical CT pulmonary angiography showed a weblike filling defect and other findings consistent with CTEPH. Coronary catheterization showed normal coronary arteries, RHC showed moderate to severe precapillary pulmonary hypertension with PVR 16.5 Wood units, and pulmonary angiography showed segmental and subsegmental chronic thrombotic disease.

She was started on riociguat and anticoagulation given low cardiac output, marked elevation of PVR and severe functional limitation. She later underwent PTE given ongoing elevated right-sided pressures despite medical therapy, then experienced prolonged respiratory insufficiency for which RHC-PA angiography found no identifiable therapies to improve oxygenation or decrease pulmonary pressures. RHC 4 months after PTE showed no significant change.

Adenosine stress perfusion CMR was performed for research purposes approximately 1 month before PTE and 1 year after PTE. Stress biventricular MBF and MPR were significantly reduced before PTE; PTE did not lead to an improvement in LV or RV perfusion, and functional parameters did not improve after PTE.

article_limitations: Table S1 (right heart catheterization values for both cases) is cited by the text but is not in source.json; it is the third page of the supplement PDF and is transcribed only in the supplement sidecar.
Values printed inside Figure 1 (MBF, MPR, EDV, ESV, SV, EF) are not article text and are recorded only in visual.json, not as annotation facts.
Control group values in the discussion (stress LV MBF, RV MBF, LV MPR, RV MPR) are comparison cohort values and are not copied to either patient.

The abstract, key points, introduction and discussion refer to "one" patient improving and "the other" not improving without naming the case; only case-labelled paragraphs are assigned to individuals.
No dates or ages are printed for the events in the article text; times are literal relative phrases such as "1 year after PTE".
